chapter_theme: The body does not last: kings die like everyone, wedding drums turn into funeral drums, and the body is a bubble, a passing cloud or dew on grass that the life within leaves behind. Because of this, the body should be used for its proper fruit, virtue and service, while it lasts.
structure_note: Death's reach (21) and the sun as the measure of days (22) open the chapter; 23-26 dwell on funerals and the indifference of the corpse; 27-30 give images of the body's brevity, three of them with a call to act now.

21.reading: Even kings who rode on elephants under umbrellas like the moon rising over a hill have been carried off and spoken of as dead; no one in this world has been left over.
21.nuance: Mudaliar takes தூற்றப்பட்டார் as 'were disparaged by many', while Pope has 'had their names proclaimed' and Shanmuganar 'spoken of lightly'; whether the dead kings are mocked or merely announced is left open by the verb.

22.reading: Because the bright sun, as the measure of one's days, rises without missing a day, do ஒப்புரவு before your days run out; no one stays on the earth beyond them.
22.nuance: ஒப்புரவு is the Kural's word for serving the community with one's means; Mudaliar cites Parimelazhagar's definition. He also says some read the last line in strained ways, without giving them. Pope's translation of this quatrain is attached to 21 in the source.

23.reading: The drums that sounded through the hall as wedding drums may sound that same day, in that same place, as funeral drums for the bridegroom; seeing this, the minds of the worthy hold fast to the way of escape.
23.nuance: The same instruments serve both rites; the verse makes the reversal one of meaning, not of sound. Shanmuganar names the way of escape as virtue.

24.reading: The drummers beat once on arrival, wait a little and beat again, and at the third beat the corpse is covered and the fire taken up; the dying carry the dead.
24.nuance: நன்றேகாண் ('fine, see!') is sarcasm for Mudaliar and a question, 'is such a life good?', for Shanmuganar; either way the last line carries the point, that the bearers are already on the same road.

25.reading: To the one who sees kin wailing in crowds as a corpse is carried to the burning ground, yet marries and believes there is joy here, the funeral drum answers with its டொண் டொண் டொண்.
25.nuance: The poem sets the man's 'உண்டு உண்டு உண்டு' (there is, there is) against the drum's 'டொண் டொண் டொண்'; Mudaliar calls the drum's reply a poetic fancy. Pope's 'mocks his vain utterance' paraphrases that echo.

26.reading: Once the dancer who stayed in this skin bag and did its work has left, what does it matter whether the body is dragged off with a rope, buried with care, thrown anywhere or reviled by many?
26.nuance: The life is a performer and the body a costume; once it has gone, the treatment of the remains has no meaning. Mudaliar lists several readings of ஊட்டும், among them the life enjoying, or being made to enjoy, the fruit of its deeds.

27.reading: Who on this wide earth equals those firm in understanding who see this body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts again and again, and resolve to end their wandering?
27.nuance: 'Again and again' (பல்காலும்) suggests repeated births as well as the bubble's quickness, and Mudaliar takes தடுமாற்றம் as the confusion of births. Shanmuganar reads it as worldly confusion.

28.reading: Those who have a sturdy body should take the fruit that body can yield, for it appears like mist on a hill and departs there without staying.
28.nuance: The verse does not despise the body here; it treats it as a means whose use must be taken quickly. Shanmuganar names the fruit as virtue.

29.reading: Knowing that the body lasts like water on the tip of a blade of grass, do virtuous deeds right now, for people say 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone'.
29.nuance: The four verbs compress a death into one breath of speech, the way it will be reported; Mudaliar supplies 'the body' as the subject of நிலையாமை.

30.reading: Unasked they come and appear in the home as kin, and wordlessly they go, leaving the body to their own people as a bird flies far off leaving its nesting tree.
30.nuance: The double வாளாதே (silently) frames a life with two unannounced events, arrival and departure; family is a place of passage.

links.note: Both use the phrase வீழ்நாள் படா- for a day not lost. In the Kural it is the good deed done daily; here it is the sun that never fails to rise and so measures out a life. The same words point to opposite sides of the account.
Both make the sun the measuring vessel of one's days; in 7 Death does the measuring and eating, in 22 the measure alone is warning enough to do ஒப்புரவு.
The funeral drum sounds in both: in 6 it may sound tomorrow for the hoarder, in 23 it replaces the wedding drum on the same day.
Both treat the life as a temporary occupant of the body, a lodger in the Kural and a dancer in a skin bag here, so the body is not its home.
Both join seeing impermanence to ending the round of births; on Mudaliar's reading of தடுமாற்றம், the wise here resolve to end what Kural 349 says ends when attachment ends.
Both say the rare body must be used to win its fruit before it goes; 34 names that fruit as virtue and adds the sugar-cane image.
Kural 336 says one here yesterday is gone today; this quatrain shrinks the span to a sentence, stood, sat, lay down, gone, and draws the command to act now.
Both picture the life leaving the body as a bird leaving its nest. The Kural makes it a comment on body and life; the Naladiyar applies it to kinsfolk, who leave the body behind for their family.

new_concepts.gloss: the body, as a perishable and impure frame
new_concepts.label_source: The verses use யாக்கை (18, 27, 28, 30, 34) and the chapter title யாக்கை நிலையாமை.

source_issues: Quatrain 21: Pope's text runs on into his translation of quatrain 22 ('Time is fleeting, use it ...'), and quatrain 22 has no Pope translation aligned.
Quatrain 30: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 30: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
